<!-- markdownlint-disable -->

## Overview

**Problem.** With an EAGLE/MTP draft model and `mamba_cache_mode="align"`, the native CPU `OffloadingConnector` never serves a partial tail. So every hit from the CPU tier stops at a scheduler-block boundary, and the tokens after it are computed again.

**Fix, in three parts:**
1. **Lookup:** look up the tail at the EAGLE proof position, as Mooncake does since #60695.
2. **Store:** fix the store gate. Before, it always skipped the one step that can store the tail.
3. **Store policy:** store an EAGLE tail only for a request that loaded from the CPU tier. Without this, parts 1 and 2 double the GPU → CPU traffic, and serving gets slower (P95 TTFT 13 % higher without it in a same-day control, see Validation).

**Result** (8 × A100, MLPerf agentic, 3 × 60 min per arm): no serving regression; SLO pass 92.42 % against 91.70 % without this PR. The CPU-tier hits now end at partial tails, as designed.

Related: #60533 (core proof), #52832 (producer partial tails), #54165 (a different bug in the same file).

## Claims

- With an EAGLE group and align Mamba, a CPU-tier hit can now end at `prefix_match_unit` granularity, as a GPU prefix-cache hit already does. Before, it ended at a whole scheduler block, minus one more block for the EAGLE pop.
- The EAGLE group's tail is keyed at `boundary + eagle_proof_margin`, the same proof that core uses since #60533. Mamba groups and non-EAGLE groups stay keyed at the boundary.
- The tail is stored on the step that computes the proof.
- With an EAGLE group, only a request that loaded from the CPU tier stores its partial tail.
- No change without an EAGLE group, or where partial tails are not supported (DCP > 1, `blocks_per_chunk > 1`, mixed block sizes, sliding-window groups). No new config option.

## Validation

### Serving A/B

**Setup.** Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8 (36 GDN + 12 full-attention layers + 1 MTP layer), TP8 + EP on 8 × A100-SXM4-40GB, MTP 3, scheduler block 800 tokens, `prefix_match_unit` 16, `--kv-offloading-backend native --kv-offloading-size 256`. MLPerf agentic multi-turn workload, 20 concurrent sessions, 3 × 60 min per arm, same node type.

**SLO** (Artificial Analysis percentile convention): **P95 TTFT ≤ 2.93 s** and **P95 TPOT ≤ 21.74 ms** (that is, P5 output speed ≥ 46 tokens/s). "SLO pass" below is the share of requests that meet both limits. The SLO holds when SLO pass ≥ 95 %.

| Arm | SLO pass, run 1 / 2 / 3 | Mean | Goodput | CPU → GPU load (whole run) | GPU prefix hit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Without this PR | 92.01 / 90.92 / 92.18 % | 91.70 % | 1.866 req/s | — | — |
| Parts 1 + 2 only (tail stored on every turn) | 85.2 / 87.3 / 87.2 % | 86.6 % | 1.67–1.72 req/s | 19.9 TB | 79.0 % |
| **This PR** (parts 1 + 2 + 3) | 93.49 / 91.93 / 91.84 % | **92.42 %** | **1.922 req/s** | **16.0 TB** | **85.2 %** |

The gain of this PR over "without" (+0.7 points, +3 % goodput) is within about two repeat spreads. So I claim no regression, not a speed-up. The "This PR" arm ran a backport on vLLM 81198e97 with the store policy behind an opt-in flag. On this model every partial tail is an EAGLE tail, so that flag gives the same rule as this PR's default.

**Same-day control (15 Oct, one node, 1 × 60 min per arm, same setup).** The "parts 1 + 2 only" arm above ran on another day; on the same day and node as this PR the gap is smaller:

| Store rule | GPU → CPU store per request | Requests done | Output tok/s per GPU | TTFT P50 / P95 | TPOT P50 / P95 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Parts 1 + 2 only (no store gate) | 247 MB | 7,450 | 111.7 | 949 / 2,297 ms | 14.07 / 23.41 ms |
| Store gate `num_locally_computed_tokens >= boundary` (review suggestion) | 247 MB | 7,490 | 111.6 | 935 / 2,203 ms | 14.16 / 23.07 ms |
| **This PR** (store only after a load from the CPU tier) | **126 MB** | **7,721** | **113.6** | 924 / **2,025 ms** | **13.69 / 22.56 ms** |

Part 3 halves the stores and, against no gate, lowers P95 TTFT by 12 % and P95 TPOT by 4 % (one run per arm). The "−5 points" of the 3 × 60 table is not reproduced on a single day; treat it as an upper bound. The review-suggested gate rarely applies here: the stored tail is past the request's GPU prefix hit.

<details>
<summary>Why parts 1 + 2 alone are slower (earlier A/B)</summary>

| Measure | Without this PR | Parts 1 + 2 only |
|---|---|---|
| CPU-tier hit tokens mod 800 | 0 in all snapshots | not 0 (e.g. 224): partial tails are served |
| SLO pass, run 1 / 2 / 3 | 90.0 / 89.2 / 89.5 % | 75.1 / 79.3 / 79.9 % |
| Goodput | 1.83–1.89 req/s | 1.31–1.43 req/s |
| P95 / P99 TTFT | 2.22–2.35 / 3.13–3.58 s | 2.94–4.18 / 5.5–13.9 s |
| P50 / P95 TPOT | 14.1–14.3 / 23.9–24.5 ms | 15.7–16.4 / 29.0–34.0 ms |
| MTP mean acceptance length | 2.676 | 2.676 |
| GPU → CPU store bytes / time | 3.00 TB / 3,814 s | 6.93 TB / 8,196 s |
| Scheduler lookup time (sum) | 1.3 s | 8.4 s |

The tails work: they are stored, found and loaded, and the drafter is unchanged. But each turn stores one new tail block (800 tokens, about 6 MB) in every KV group. Most requests hit the GPU prefix cache on the next turn, so most of these stores are never read. Tail stores were 18,650 (about one per request) and 64.5 % of the 6.93 TB stored. Part 3 removes these stores.

How the bug was found: without this PR, `vllm:external_prefix_cache_hits_total` was an exact multiple of 800 in all 17 snapshots of two 3-hour runs (example: 402,580,800 = 503,226 × 800). With part 1 only, it was still a multiple of 800. That pointed to the store gate.

</details>

### Unit tests

All in `tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector/test_scheduler.py`:

| What | Tests |
|---|---|
| Proof key: store and lookup | `test_eagle_proof_margin_follows_core_hit_alignment`, `test_eagle_partial_tail_store_keys_attention_at_proof`, `test_eagle_partial_lookup_loads_attention_proof` |
| Store gate (part 2): round trip | `test_eagle_partial_tail_round_trip_serves_mamba_checkpoint[True]`: fails with part 1 only, passes with part 2 |
| Store only when the proof is in the prompt | `test_eagle_partial_tail_store_needs_proof_in_prompt` (5 cases) |
| Popped chunk looked up once | `test_eagle_partial_lookup_probes_popped_chunk_once` (6 lookups instead of 7; 7 instead of 9) |
| Store policy (part 3) | `test_eagle_partial_tail_store_needs_offload_load` ([False] and [True] cases) |

| Run | Result |
|---|---|
| A100 (CUDA), nightly 5555a2d8 image, whole `offloading_connector/` | 589 passed, 0 failed. With #61375 also applied: 590 passed. |
| macOS (CPU), whole `offloading_connector/` | 476 passed. The same 105 failures occur with and without this PR; they are macOS platform errors (`Hybrid KV cache manager ... not supported`, `Invalid device string: ':0'`). |
| `ruff check`, `ruff format --check` (ruff 0.14.0) | clean |

```bash
python -m pytest -q tests/v1/kv_connector/unit/offloading_connector/
```

This PR and #61375 (a different bug in `offloading/scheduler.py`) merge without conflicts.

## Details

**Root cause 1: lookup.** `SchedulerOffloadConfig.from_spec` set `supports_partial_tail = False` when any group was an EAGLE group. For an EAGLE group, the complete-chunk lookup asks for one extra chunk and then drops it. So the hit ended one scheduler block before the last stored chunk, and no partial tail was tried.

**Root cause 2: store gate.**
1. With EAGLE block drop, core stops the prefill at the Mamba checkpoint T = floor(P/h)·h − h.
2. On the next step (tokens T..P), the state is copied (CoW), and the manager hands `(group, cow_block, T)` to the connector one time.
3. The scheduler builds the connector metadata before `_update_after_schedule`, so `num_computed_tokens == T` at that point.
4. So the gate `boundary + margin > num_computed_tokens` reads `T + h > T`. This is always true, so the store is always skipped, and the hand-off does not come again.

**Changes.**
- Remove the EAGLE exclusion from `supports_partial_tail`.
- Key the EAGLE non-recurrent groups at `boundary + margin` in store, lookup and load.
- Margin rule as in core: one hash unit if `cache_hit_alignment_tokens` < block and the group manager supports fine-grained lookup; else one block.
- Widen the partial search by one block, with bridge keys for the dropped chunk. That chunk is looked up once per lookup; a miss skips that block.
- Check the proof against `min(num_computed_tokens + num_scheduled_tokens[req_id], num_prompt_tokens)`. The cap keeps the proof out of speculative tokens.
- With an EAGLE group, store a partial tail only if `update_state_after_alloc` scheduled a CPU-tier load for this request (`RequestOffloadState.loaded_from_offload`). Complete chunks and aligned boundary states are stored as before.

**Why the proof-step store is safe.** Stores are only queued in `wait_for_save` and are sent at the start of the next step. The CPU transfer stream waits on the compute stream at that point, so the copy runs after this step's forward wrote the proof block.

**Difference from #60695.** Mooncake stores one key per hash unit. The native connector stores whole chunks and keeps its chunk-level EAGLE drop for complete chunks. So only the partial-tail key of EAGLE groups changes.

**Limitations.**
- If the hand-off step stops before `T + h`, the tail is not stored. I ran core's chunk-split code on 20,000 prompts (1k–200k tokens) per configuration. No hand-off was lost when block ≤ `max_num_batched_tokens` with EAGLE or single-module MTP. Losses occur only with multi-module MTP (0.2–0.45 %) or with a block larger than the token budget (≤ 1.7 %). A fix would need core to keep the CoW block across steps; not done.
- The store policy is a heuristic. A request served only from the GPU prefix cache stores no EAGLE tail. If the GPU later evicts that prefix, the next turn's CPU-tier hit ends at the last complete chunk. That turn then loads from the CPU tier and stores its tail, so the turn after it can get a partial hit. Measured on one workload only.
- When the dropped chunk is present, the search covers two blocks. This applies only with an EAGLE group.
- Existing CPU caches hold no EAGLE tails, so no migration is needed.

**Size:** `offloading/scheduler.py` +170 / −34 (no core files changed); tests +348 / −1.

## Details

**Root cause 1: lookup.** `SchedulerOffloadConfig.from_spec` set `supports_partial_tail = False` when any group was an EAGLE group. For an EAGLE group, the complete-chunk lookup asks for one extra chunk and then drops it. So the hit ended one scheduler block before the last stored chunk, and no partial tail was tried.

**Root cause 2: store gate.**
1. With EAGLE block drop, core stops the prefill at the Mamba checkpoint T = floor(P/h)·h − h.
2. On the next step (tokens T..P), the state is copied (CoW), and the manager hands `(group, cow_block, T)` to the connector one time.
3. The scheduler builds the connector metadata before `_update_after_schedule`, so `num_computed_tokens == T` at that point.
4. So the gate `boundary + margin > num_computed_tokens` reads `T + h > T`. This is always true, so the store is always skipped, and the hand-off does not come again.

**Changes.**
- Remove the EAGLE exclusion from `supports_partial_tail`.
- Key the EAGLE non-recurrent groups at `boundary + margin` in store, lookup and load.
- Margin rule as in core: one hash unit if `cache_hit_alignment_tokens` < block and the group manager supports fine-grained lookup; else one block.
- Widen the partial search by one block, with bridge keys for the dropped chunk. That chunk is looked up once per lookup; a miss skips that block.
- Check the proof against `min(num_computed_tokens + num_scheduled_tokens[req_id], num_prompt_tokens)`. The cap keeps the proof out of speculative tokens.
- With an EAGLE group, store a partial tail only if `update_state_after_alloc` scheduled a CPU-tier load for this request (`RequestOffloadState.loaded_from_offload`). Complete chunks and aligned boundary states are stored as before.

**Why the proof-step store is safe.** Stores are only queued in `wait_for_save` and are sent at the start of the next step. The CPU transfer stream waits on the compute stream at that point, so the copy runs after this step's forward wrote the proof block.

**Difference from #60695.** Mooncake stores one key per hash unit. The native connector stores whole chunks and keeps its chunk-level EAGLE drop for complete chunks. So only the partial-tail key of EAGLE groups changes.

**Limitations.**
- If the hand-off step stops before `T + h`, the tail is not stored. I ran core's chunk-split code on 20,000 prompts (1k–200k tokens) per configuration. No hand-off was lost when block ≤ `max_num_batched_tokens` with EAGLE or single-module MTP. Losses occur only with multi-module MTP (0.2–0.45 %) or with a block larger than the token budget (≤ 1.7 %). A fix would need core to keep the CoW block across steps; not done.
- The store policy is a heuristic. A request served only from the GPU prefix cache stores no EAGLE tail. If the GPU later evicts that prefix, the next turn's CPU-tier hit ends at the last complete chunk. That turn then loads from the CPU tier and stores its tail, so the turn after it can get a partial hit. Measured on one workload only.
- When the dropped chunk is present, the search covers two blocks. This applies only with an EAGLE group.
- Existing CPU caches hold no EAGLE tails, so no migration is needed.

## Summary

This pull lets the CPU offloading connector store and serve partial tails when a model has an EAGLE or MTP draft group. The pull is marked as a draft. We found two serious and two smaller findings. The most important problem is that a hand-off skipped because the proof is not yet computed is never offered again, so that tail is never stored.

## Serious findings

**1. A skipped hand-off is lost for good [offloading/scheduler.py]**
When the EAGLE proof has not been computed by the end of the step, the code skips the copy-on-write hand-off for that step. The hand-off is created once and cleared the next time pending hand-offs are drained, so nothing retries it and that tail is never stored.
*Change:* Defer the hand-off until the proof is computed instead of dropping it.

**2. EAGLE configs double the partial-tail lookups on every request [offloading/scheduler.py]**
With an EAGLE proof margin the search covers two blocks instead of one, which doubles the boundary iterations. Each boundary also probes extra bridge keys before the per-group lookups, which adds lookups and host-to-GPU bridge loads on a path that runs for every request.
*Change:* Avoid paying the extra lookup cost on every request, for example by only probing the second block or the bridge keys when they can change the result.

Thank you for the review. I checked each point against the code.

1. **Skipped hand-off.** This is correct: a hand-off without the proof is not offered again. I measured how often it happens. I ran vLLM's own chunk-split code (`_mamba_block_aligned_split`, `_reserve_prefill_lookahead`) on 20,000 prompts of 1k–200k tokens for each configuration. With block ≤ `max_num_batched_tokens` and EAGLE or single-module MTP, the loss was 0 in all 24 configurations. A chunk that starts at the checkpoint ends either at the prompt end or at the next block boundary, and both are at least one hash unit past it. Otherwise the request is not scheduled on that step. Losses occur only with multi-module MTP (0.2–0.45 %) or with a block larger than the token budget (up to 1.7 %). A deferral needs core to hold the CoW block across steps, and it changes the hand-off contract for Mooncake and `simple_kv_offload`. Mooncake uses the same gate. I kept the skip and documented the limit in the description.
2. **Lookup cost.** Fixed in `87e15691d`. The popped chunk is looked up once for each lookup, and a miss skips the boundaries that need it. The results do not change: a differential check over 20,000 random key states found 0 differences and 17 % fewer lookups. I kept the second block when the popped chunk is ready, because a hit there is longer than any hit in the first block.

I kept one inline lookup for a non-EAGLE, non-CoW group that never queried the bridge chunk (its prefix lookup can stop at an aligned `complete_boundary`, e.g. when the Mamba alignment is larger than the block size). If you are fine with treating that chunk as a miss, the lookup loop and its event records can go too.

@orozery, first result for your store gate (`num_locally_computed_tokens >= boundary`), on the same setup as the PR body (C20, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8, TP8 + EP, MTP 3, native CPU offload 256 GiB, 8 × A100). It ran behind an opt-in flag on the same backport.

GPU → CPU stores per finished request (`kv_offload_store_bytes_total` / `request_success_total`, final metrics snapshot of each server):

| Store rule | Store per request | Runs |
|---|---|---|
| No gate (parts 1 + 2) | 250 MB | 3 × 60 min |
| Your gate | 247 MB | 1 × 60 min |
| This PR (store only after a load from the CPU tier) | 129 MB | 3 × 60 min |

So in this workload your gate skips almost no stores. The tail that is stored lies past the request's GPU prefix hit (it is in the new tokens of the turn), so `num_locally_computed_tokens` is almost never at or past the boundary.

The SLO effect is not settled yet: the three arms did not run on the same day and node, and I see a day-to-day difference that I cannot explain yet. I am running a same-day control (no gate and this PR, one node, one job) and will post the SLO comparison here.

@orozery, the same-day control is done. All three store rules ran on one node on the same day (15 Oct), 1 × 60 min each at C20, same setup as before:

| Store rule | GPU → CPU store per request | Requests done | Output tok/s per GPU | TTFT P50 / P95 | TPOT P50 / P95 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| No gate (parts 1 + 2) | 247 MB | 7,450 | 111.7 | 949 / 2,297 ms | 14.07 / 23.41 ms |
| Your gate (`num_locally_computed_tokens >= boundary`) | 247 MB | 7,490 | 111.6 | 935 / 2,203 ms | 14.16 / 23.07 ms |
| This PR (store only after a load from the CPU tier) | 126 MB | 7,721 | 113.6 | 924 / 2,025 ms | 13.69 / 22.56 ms |

- Your gate stores as much as no gate in this workload, and its SLO result is within run-to-run noise of no gate.
- The after-load rule halves the GPU → CPU stores and, against no gate on the same day, lowers P95 TTFT by 272 ms (−12 %) and P95 TPOT by 0.85 ms (−4 %), with about 4 % more requests done.
- Correction to the PR body: it said that parts 1 + 2 alone lose 5 points (86.6 % vs 91.70 %). That number came from runs on another day and node; the no-gate arm did not reproduce it on the same day (SLO pass 90.59 %, against 92.67 % for this PR). I have updated the description. One run per arm, so this is a direction, not a precise size.

So part 3 still carries a measurable part of the result, but less than I first wrote. I am fine either way on the split: keep it here, or move store admission to its own PR that lands first.
